The House resumed from April 12 consideration in Committee of Bill No. 12, respecting the election of members of the House of Commons and the electoral franchise.-Hon. Mr. Guthrie.
Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 87-effect of corrupt practices, disqualification, etc.
Is the period of disqualification here the same as in the present law?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
In the Act at present in force the disqualification period is eight years. Before that law was enacted the disqualification period was seven years. I think it well to fix the period at seven years and make all the provisions of our law conform. I therefore move that the word "eight" be struck out and the word "seven" inserted.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 88-Candidates not convicted unless corrupt practice done by himself, agent, or with his knowledge-Proviso.
Does this Bill give any definition of "other agent?"

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no definition of agent for the purposes of this section. What is done has to be done with the candidate's knowledge. It is knowledge of the candidate which practically constitutes agency under the section. The old section, which was number 277, contained a provision similar to this, namely:

A candidate shall not he liable, nor shall his election be voided, for any unlawful act under the two sections next preceding committed by his agent other than his official agent.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 89-Election not avoided unless illegal practices by candidate, agent, etc.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This section and the three or four preceding sections are very much in the nature of new legislation, and they all seem to be framed with the object of protecting the candidate against extreme or unnecessary actions. Has the minister any explanation to give to the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I have no special information to give. The sections are, I think, a little more Skillfully drawn than the former section in regard to the effect of an act by agents. The idea is to draw a distinction between acts of the candidate, acts of the official agent, and acts of some other person who legally becomes an agent through taking part in an eleotion with the knowledge of the candidate. The old section did not make that distinction, but just provided, that a candidate should not be liable nor should his eleotion be voided for any unlawful act under the preceding two sections-which were the sections dealing with illegal and corrupt practices- committed by his agent other than his official agent. If an agent not the official agent, acting with the knowledge of the candidate, contravenes the provisions of this Act, a penalty is attached, and the penalties attached by these two or three sections do not interfere with any of the provisions of the Contraverted Elections Act. The election may at the same time be set aside. These sections deal only with the penalties that shall be imposed.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 92-Recovery of penalties and forfeitures-Imprisonment for non-payment, etc.

Instead of giving security for costs it would to my mind be more simple to make the plaintiff deposit the fifty dollars in court, and perhaps the amount should be increased to one hundred dollars. Oftentimes actions are dictated not by love of the law but by hate, and such actions should not be encouraged.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know how it is in the province of Quebec where my hon. friend comes from, but in Ontario and, I

think, in all the other provinces the order for security is always satisfied with cash; one can deposit the cash in court instead of giving security. The old section has been in our law for a long time.
The giving of security does not necessarily involve a deposit in cash.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: But it permits it.
Would it not he better to make the deposit compulsory?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I would prefer to leave . the section as it is.

I notice in subsection 6 the burden of proof, contrary to the ordinary rules, is shifted to the defendant. If he is charged with having voted where he had no right to vote, the onus is upon him to prove that he was entitled to vote there. In several places throughout this Act there is a departure from the principle that every one accused of an offence is presumed to be innocent until the contrary is proved. Further, there is nothing here about where the venue shall be. I submit that in all these proceedings the venue should be in the county in which the election was held. There should also be some provision for the production as evidence of the list, duly certified by the clerk of the municipality, which should be prima facie' evidence of the fact that the name of the accused was on the list and that he had the right to vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
It might be convenient to have all these actions brought in the county in which the cause of action arose. But in our Ontario county courts it is not essential that the actions should be tried in the county in which the cause of action arose. There is, however, a rule of the court that this shall be done wherever possible, and I take it that that rule would apply to an action for recovery under one of the sections of this Act. My hon. friend will notice that the penalty may be the subject of action in a court of competent jurisdiction in the province in which the cause of action arises. If Ontario was the province in question, the court of competent jurisdiction would be a court of the particular county in which the offence was committed, unless the parties did not reside in that county. If the parties resided in another county, there would be another jurisdiction for the trial of that action. I assume that the jurisdiction of the various county and district courts throughout Canada is limited by rules applicable to the
courts of the provinces. As to the burden of proof so far as the right to vote is concerned, I do not think there is any great hardship. The accused knows the facts and he can immediately inform the eourt as to his right to vote, whereas the complainant may have very great difficulty in establishing that fact.

I cannot agree with my hon. friend's law as to the simplicity of the evidence. If a man is charged with having voted when his name is not on the list, the evidence of the existence of his right is in writing, on the list. The judge will not accept secondary evidence; he must produce the best evidence; therefore the list, properly certified by the county clerk, should be produced to prove that his name is on it and that he therefore has the right to vote. As to the venue, cases of this kind sufficiently partake of criminality to justify the affording to the accused of all the protection which is afforded to a criminal. Any person who is charged with a criminal offence must be tried in the county in which he resides and in which the cause of action arose. Why should not that be the ease here?

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 93-no privileged excuse from answering questions:
Does that include any knowledge that a lawyer may possess, having received the same in confidence from a client?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: This has been the law for a long time. I should think that the recognized privilege which exists between a lawyer and his client, within the limitations established by law, would still exist. While I should not like to change the language of the section, I unhesitatingly give that as my own view of the matter.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 94-production of election, etc., not required in suits:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The Assistant Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, who has gone over this Bill with a great deal of care, has suggested that in clause 94 and in some other clauses, some of which have already been passed, the words "election papers" should be used to include practically all papers used at an election and that a definition of the term should be inserted in clause 2. For my part I do not quite see the feasibility of the suggestion, but I merely men-

tion it as later on we may in considering clause 2 adopt the suggestion and place a definition of the term "election papers" in that clause. If we do that, clause 94 would require some slight amendment, but in the meantime, I prefer the clause as it is now. It is the same as the old one.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 100-advance voting by railway employees, sailors, etc.:

This is a very long and rather elaborate clause. The aim is one with which we all sympathize, I am sure. It is to provide that a commercial traveller, a railway employee, a sailor, or any other voter who in the ordinary pursuit of his vocation is obliged to be absent at the time of of the election shall not lose his vote, and provision is made whereby he may vote at what is called an advance poll. I want to offer a suggestion to the minister which I think is worthy of his consideration. The purpose of this provision is undoubtedly a good one, but it seems to me the machinery is very elaborate and must be very expensive. Why could not provision be made, as in the case of a joint stock company, for instance, to let the few voters, because they will be few in proportion to the total electorate, who would avail themselves of this provision vote by proxy? There may be a giving away of the secrecy of the vote *by that method, but only to a very small extent indeed. Why could not a sailor or a railway employee who happens to be away empower his brother, or cousin, or sister, or mother, or anybody else, to vote for him? The only objection that can be offered to that is the lack of secrecy, but as a matter of fact nine men out of ten make no secrecy as to how they intend to vote. I think the suggestion is worthy of the minister's consideration. The machinery provided here is elaborate and expensive, and I think the same good end could be served at much less expense by allowing these men to vote by proxy. I need not elaborate the argument, but I would ask the minister to consider whether it is not a proper suggestion.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I have had one discussion on this matter, and there is one very large body of the people of this country, the railroad people, who do not like the proxy idea. I think the ordinary man looks upon the right to vote as something in the nature of a sacred right, as something which he should not delegate to any third party, but as a right which he should exercise for himself. The only person with whom I have 
discussed this question were the railroan men, and they were very strongly opposed to the idea of voting by proxy. No matter what the cost may be or how great the inconvenience, the men claim the right to vote, and that arrangements should be made, if at all possible, to that end. I can quite see that the suggestion of my hon. friend has this merit, that it would save a great deal of expense to the country, but I think the object to be attained, namely, that all classes of people shall have the' right to exercise their franchise, justifies us in going to a great deal of expense.
I might say that there are some suggested amendments to this clause. I have had suggestions, f6r instance, from the Commercial Travellers' Association, and from various railway brotherhoods in Canada. I do not know whether it would be well to discuss this clause fully to-day. We might or might not, just as the committee sees fit. It is a clause that will have to be amended to some extent.

We all agree that the secrecy of the vote should be protected, but it is a very practical world we are living in to-day, and nine men out of ten make no secret of how they intend to vote. The man who does make a secret of it is quite the exception, so I do not think the argument as to secrecy should apply at all. I have no doubt that the first impression of the railway men would be that they wanted the right to vote themselves, but I think [DOT]if we had a deputation of the men from the railway service they would admit the reasonableness of this suggestion, and I venture to say that nearly every man in the railway seryice who intends to vote makes no secret of how he is going to vote, but tells his friends that he is going to vote Grit or Tory or Farmer, or for one of the other numerous groups that are springing up.

Will the hon. gentleman say how he knows that a man is going to vote a certain way? A voteT may say all sorts of things before an election that are simply camouflage, and may vote just the opposite way to what he said he was going to vote.
Not in Nova Scotia.

We are not accustomed to that class of voter down my way. I am speaking in all seriousness. I grant that there is some force in the argument that a man has the right to vote himself, but I say that for the object in view

the machinery is too expensive and too elaborate. I am not quarrelling with the expense only, although that is a consideration. To create this elaborate machinery to give a comparatively small number of men the right to vote is like creating a steam engine to run a canoe. There is nothing to justify such expensive machinery for such a simple purpose.

I am not much in
sympathy with the idea of voting by proxy. My hon. friend says that he has discussed this matter with the railway brotherhoods and has received communications with respect to it from commercial travellers' associations and other bodies. There is no class which has been pressing for legislation of this kind for a number of years so strongly as the commercial travellers, but I am quite sure that a large number of them will not 'be able to avail themselves of this provision. A large number of commercial travellers go on a two or three weeks' trip. I know, for instance, commer- >
cial travellers in the city of Quebec who leave for the Gaspe coast or the Lake St. John district who would not be able to avail themselves of this provision, becaus^ three days is not sufficient time to allow. If the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) is not accepted, I would ask the minister to provide a longer period than three days, which I do not think is sufficient to give the commercial travellers and the other class who are asking for this legislation the privilege they desire.

I have been requested
many times during the past year to bring before the House at the earliest opportunity the question of voting by mail. This proposition is endorsed by the Commercial Travellers' Association, and no doubt the minister in charge of the Bill has received from them representations in the matter. The hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), very wisely pointed out that the time provided for in this Act is not adequate, and certainly three days will not afford the commercial travellers of the country sufficient time in which to exercise , the franchise. There can be no doubt in the mind of any hon. gentleman that the Commercial Travellers' Association represents possibly the most intelligent section of the community.
Hear, hear.

There is no body of men who have a better knowledge of the affairs of the country than the commercial travellers, who come in close contact with the 75
people of every constituency from coast to coast. Some hon. gentlemen said " hear, hear" a moment ago by way of comment on my statement that the commercial travellers are among the best informed citizens of the country. However that comment may be interpreted, I repeat the assertion and I will go a step further and say that the commercial travellers are better informed on public matters than any other class of people in the Dominion, without a single exception. This body comprises over 30,000 men, who all take a keen interest in the nation's affairs; and it would be impossible for them to take advantage of the provisions of this Act, worded as it is. I would therefore strongly urge upon the minister the necessity of providing for voting by mail. Many of these travellers leave on extended trips covering a period very often of six months. The commercial travellers cover the Dominion twice in the twelve months and it seems to me that there should be some provision for their accommodation in the matter of voting. But the commercial travellers are not the only citizens whose convenience is involved in this proposition. There are the sailors, who are sometimes away from home for months and months together. Then there are the lumbermen, the most difficult body of men to deal with in any election, and hon. members who have had experience in this direction can bear me out; and another class of men who encounter great obstacles in any attempt to record their votes are the miners. So that for the convenience of this considerable portion of the population-the commercial travellers, the sailors, the lumbermen, and the miners, to say nothing of the railroad men,-I think it is the duty of the Acting Solicitor General very seriously to consider the proposal I made. I quite realize that there will be attendant difficulties in connection with such a provision, but these are no greater than the difficulties that would surround the proposition which is before the House at the present time. I trust, Mr. Chairman, that the minister will give due consideration to the representations that have been made to him, through me, and I have no doubt directly, by the commercial travellers.

In regard to
the observations of the hon. member for Queen's and Shelburne (Mr. Fielding), I do not think that hon. gentleman bears in mind the fact that the provisions of the Act applying to a class of men who, in many constituencies in Canada, constitute the majority of the voters. There are several constituencies of which I have personal



knowledge, where some four or five thousand men will be affected by this clause, and to ask that such a large number of men should vote by proxy seems to me to be beyond what any reasonable man would demand in connectidn with the exercise of the franchise. Then, with regard to the complicated machinery that has been set up. the difficulty of carrying out the provisions of this clause, the expense, etc., I think the clause is in reality very similar to the provisions under which the railway employees and commercial travellers were allowed to vote in the last provincial election in Ontario. Boiled down, it means that there shall be in each constituency one advance poll man to be deputy returning officer and poll clerk, and there shall be issuance of certificates by the registrar or the enumerator, as the case may be, to enable these men to vote. I think that any suggestion to the railway employees, to say nothing of all the other men who will be affected, that they should vote by proxy would only be tantamount to saying " We are not going to give you the privilege of exercising the franchise;" because these men will not avail themselves of such a privilege.

I would suggest an
amendment to the clause to provide for elections on a specified day, so that men in every calling in life might have an opportunity of exercising the privileges of citizenship. I do not see any sound reason why we should not have the general election fixed by statute to take place on a Monday, say. Every travelling agent is at home, if not every Sunday, at least every second or third Sunday, and if he knew that the election would take place on a certain Monday he would so arrange his itinerary as to be home on the Sunday preceding election day. In the province of New Brunswick we have such a privilege to accommodate sailors and fishermen. Before Confederation a statute provided that elections should always be held on Monday in the constituency of Gloucester, which I have the honour to represent, and which is one of the largest constituencies in the Maritime Provinces. This provision was made to meet the convenience of the fishermen in this constituency, who comprise a very large propor.-tion of the electorate. They generally leave home on Monday, returning on Saturday nights, and the provision is a very convenient one. There is a tendency in New Brunswick to-day to have the general provincial election held on Monday, and I would not be astonished if this suggestion

took the form of legislation before long. If the election were held on Monday every class of citizens, including railway employees, would make preparations in view of the fact, and I have no doubt whatever that the majority of them would be able to exercise the franchise. Railway men could vote* early in the morning and late in the evening. In that way, as suggested by the hon. member for Queen's and Shelburne, w*e could dispense with this clause, which will undoubtedly involve a great deal of expenditure, or at least considerably more than would be entailed if the election were held on Monday. I think the committee should weigh well this suggestion, which is an important one.
Mr. J. E, ARMSTRONG: Before this clause is disposed pf II would like the Acting Solicitor General to take into consideration the fact that our inland sailors would be strongly opposed to voting by proxy. Not many days ago a delegation of masters and mates waited upon me in regard to this very subject, and urged the importance of placing before the Acting Solicitor General the need of enacting just stich a clause as is contained in this Bill.
I am also satisfied that the representatives of the railway brotherhoods and the commercial travellers would be strongly opposed to a clause compelling them to vote by proxy.

I presume the idea of the Acting Solicitor General in moving this clause is to give every elector in Canada a chance to vote. The idea is a good one but I really cannot see how it is going to be carried out successfully. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat spoke about the position of the lake sailors. Well, they would be able to vote in three ways. But, in my opinion, it would be most unfair to allow railway employees and commercial travellers who are away from home to vote, and not provide some means whereby our sailors and fishermen in the Maritime Provinces and British Columbia, who may be away from home for perhaps a week, two weeks, or two months before election day, could exercise the franchise. If some scheme cannot be devised whereby every man in Canada who was away from home might vote, I would say let the old law remain in force and only permit those who are at home on election day to poll their votes.

-Supplementing the remarks I have already made, I desire to

place on Hansard a resolution which I have received from the Commercial Travellers' Association upon this subject. It is very brief and will not take long to read.

speechtext: The House resumed in Committee on Bill No. 12 respecting the election of members of the House of Commons and the electoral franchise.-Mr. Guthrie. Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the Committee rose to receive the message from His Excellency the Administrator we were considering clause 100. Mr. Pedlow had the floor.

Mr. Speaker, when the House was called to order for the purpose of adjourning to the Senate I was about to ask permission to place on Hansard some resolutions I had received from commercial travellers' associations of Canada. The Dominion Commercial Travellers' Association of the City of Montreal passed the following resolution:
This association has been informed that it is the intention of the House to bring a Bill before Parliament making provision for a system of "Votes by Mail." The board of directors of this association are heartily in favour of the proposition, and trust that Parliament will see its way clear to have the system adopted. As you are no doubt aware, there are about 30,000 commercial travellers in Canada, and it is rather hard on these men that they should not have the opportunity of voting simply by reason of the fact that their business necessitates their being , absent from their home town on the day of the poll. These men are represent-75J	'
ing many and varied interests, and the very nature of their work qualifies them to vote intelligently on the matters most affecting the economic welfare of the Dominion.
The Commercial Travellers' Association of Brockville passed this resolution:
This association heartily endorses the proposed legislation to permit commercial travellers to exercise their franchise, both for parliamentary and municipal elections, by mail when unable to vote at their own polling places on election day, and we greatly appreciate your kind interest in our behalf in this matter.
The Commercial Travellers' Association of Canada have sent me from Toronto the following resolution:
It is a matter that has been before the association since 1906, and if the voting-by-mail Bill is passed, it will only be equitable and fair to the commercial traveller and something that he will appreciate very much.
It may seem to the committee that this-is something so radical that it is impossible-of adoption, but let me tell the hon. minister who has charge of this Bill that far from being an impossible proposition, it is in operation in several countries. I understand that in the Argentine Republic voting by mail is quite common, and it is effected somewhat after this manner. Each voter being duly registered carries with him a registration card with his signature and photograph attached, and on polling day all he has to do is to go to the nearest post office, present his registration card, and obtain from the postmaster a ballot, which is enclosed in a registered envelope. Having marked his ballot he forwards it to the constituency in which he wishes to cast his vote.
I have also in my possession a 'specimen ballot used by the University of the City of Dublin for university elections, but these elections are conducted just as strictly as a parliamentary election. I shall be pleased to submit this form to the minister for in-' spection if he so desires.

As a representative of a constituency in which reside some thousands of railway men, I wish to very strongly support the proposal contained in the Bill of providing for advanced ballots. The hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) will therefore not be surprised at my opposing his suggestion that unless we can get everybody to vote we should do away with these polls. In the last provincial election these advance polls were used in Fort William, and I assume, in the smaller railway centres. The result was satisfactory to those who voted, though I confess that there may not have been so much satisfaction on the.

part of candidates who were members of the old parties. Railway men, whether engineers or firemen, conductors or brakemen, are, perhaps, among the most intelligent of the working classes of this country, and that is a very important reason why this suggestion should be done away with. In these times of unrest-unreasonable unrest in many cases-we should not do anything to interfere with the level-headed. higher class votes which these advance polls will enable to be cast. I very strongly submit, therefore, that the provision with regard to advance polls Temain very much as it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
My own view is that the idea of establishing advance polls as outlined in the clause is a very valuable one. Possibly it can be improved; in the meantime this clause had better stand.
Section stands.

Mr, McKENZTE: I notice that the language of section 36 of the old Act is not the same as that of this section. Perhaps the minister will explain the reason for not accepting the old form.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Section 36 of the old Act rt ac!:
No company or association other than one incorporated for political purposes alone shall, directly or indirectly, contribute, loan, advance, pay or promise or offer to pay any money or its equivalent to, or for, or in aid of, any candidate at an election, etc.

And subsection 2 provides that:
Every director, shareholder, officer, attorney, or agent, of any company or association violating the provisions of this section, who aids, abets, advises, or takes part in, any such violation shall be punished.
The distinction is almost in, the first line of the section, the present section 10 reading :
No unincorporated company or association and no incorporated company or association.
the old section being:
No company or association other than one incorporated for political purposes alone.
I think the idea of the draftsman has been to make it clear that the section included any companies and associations both incorporated and unincorporated, and that no such company or association, other than one incorporated for political purposes alone, should be entitled to make any contributions to elections, neither should any director, shareholder, officer, attorney or agent of a company be entitled so to contriBute.

The exception
here made is in favour of a company incorporated for political purposes. It is not necessary, it seems to me, that such an association or company should be incorporated. I presume that the object of incorporation would be publicity, but considerable expense attaches to the act of incorporation. Such an association or company would have to be incorporated by a private Act of Parliament, and if the legislature were not sitr ting when it was desired to secure incorporation great inconvenience would result. As I say, the object apparently is to have it publicly known that such a company or association is in existence, and it seems to me that that object, might be accomplished in a more simple way.
If the words "organized or" were inserted between the word "one" in the second line and the word "incorporated" in the third line the section would read:
No unincorporated company or association and no incorporated company or association other than one organized or incorporatedand I think that would be sufficient notice to the public of the fact that such company or association exists. It would also do away with the unnecessary expense of incorporating a company or association which would be active probably only once in four or five years. I would suggest the insertion of those words.
I would also suggest that some such provision as this be made:

Whenever a company or association is organized for political purposes, but not incorporated, such company or association shall, before taking any action under this section, file with the Secretary of Stateor any other official that the minister would prefer-
-a memorandum giving the name and address of such company or association and the officers thereof, and the territory in which such company or association shall operate.
I think that amendment would not only simplify the working of the Act, but it would also simplify the operation of such company or association.
While I am on my feet I may as well make some further suggestions that occur to me in regard to this section. Subsection 1 prohibits the payment of any money "in aid of any political party, committee, or association," but so far as I can see the Bill does not contain any provision for the enforcement of that prohibition; there is only a clause for enforcing the prohibition against the giving of funds to a candidate or his agent. Supposing that a man or a company or association wishes to contribute $1,000 or $10,000 to the general political fund of a party, there is nothing in this Bill, so far as I can see, to prevent it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There is nothing to prevent an individual contributing to a fund for party purposes, and' there never has been.	[DOT]

The Bill contains ample provisions to enforce penalties so far as contributions to the funds of a candidate are concerned, but so far as I can see there is nothing to compel publicity of contributions to the funds of a political party, and that is where the greatest danger comes in.
I presume that this clause was inserted primarily to prevent contributions by big incorporated companies-strong financial institutions-that might be able to improperly influence elections-and we all know the people generally do think such corporations improperly influence elections whether they actually do or not. It is very much more important that we should provide machinery to prevent this greater evil of contributions to party funds by large incorporated companies, and if we do not take steps to this end I am afraid the people will think that we are not really trying to overcome the evil.
I would like to>
make another suggestion in regard to this section. It would be well to have a further provision that any such company or association making contributions permitted by this clause shall submit

a full report thereof to the Chief Electoral Officer -within say fifteen days after the election, stating the amount of all such contributions and to whom given. Upon receipt of such statement it would be well for the Chief Electoral Officer to have a copy thereof published in the Canada Gazette and possibly in some daily newspaper. Publicity is the main thing that we are after. I do not see that much is to be gained by forbidding contributions from companies, because any such provision could readily be evaded. I do not object to the section, but I want to see it made more effective; I want to see the exceptions which we set forth here made more easily carried out. Instead of insisting upon the incorporation of every little association which wants to contribute toward the election expenses of some candidate, we should permit them to organize upon giving proper notice of such organization. Then we want publicity, and we want some machinery by which we can enforce every provision forbidding contributions from companies to the campaign funds of any party or any association.

The clause under discussion is possibly one of the most important clauses of this Bill. Most representative institutions are regarded with a certain amount of suspicion by the rank and file of the people. One of the reasons why Parliament has lost to a certain degree the influence and the importance which it should have in this country is because there is a feeling abroad which, I believe, is largely unfounded, that the members of this House have been elected by funds supplied by friends of theirs; that the large interests have had a great deal to do with electing members. If we wish to enjoy the prestige and the influence and the honour which should belong to members of this House, we must see that so far as legislation can so provide, such a condition as that shall not exist in future. I do not think that we are going to get away from it by saying that no unorganized association or no incorporated organization other than an organization created for political purposes only shall have the right to subscribe to campaign funds. Contributions to political funds are necessary; we cannot get rid of them. In certain constituencies which are very large or very populous, election expenses are incurred which candidates of moderate means cannot bear, and in such ridings it is only fair that people who have the same views as the candidate whom they
wish to support should be allowed to contribute to his election fund. I have drafted a resolution looking to the elimination of what I think may be rightly regarded as an abuse. It has two objects in view. It provides, first, that no association or company, incorporated or unincorporated, shall have the right to subscribe to a campaign fund; second, that subscriptions to campaign funds, whether general party funds or funds for individuals, shall emanate only from individuals, be of their own money, and be limited to a certain sum, which, for the purpose of argument, I shall put at $10,000.
Hear, hear.

The minister smiles, but he may find some one who, charmed by his eloquence, is prepared to put $10,000 into his campaign fund if he be a candidate in the next election. My resolution provides also that there shall be full and complete publicity as respects these campaign funds, so that the public will know just who has put up the money for the election of candidates. I therefore move, seconded by Mr. Fournier, that section 10 be struck out, and that the following be substituted therefor:
(1)	No incorporated or unincorporated company or association, nor any firm, shall directly or indirectly contribute, loan, advance, pay or promise, or offer to pay, any money or its equivalent to, or for, or in aid of, any candidate at an election, or to, or for, or in aid of any political party, committee, or association, or to, or for, or in furtherance of, any political purpose whatever, or for the indemnification or reimbursement of any person for money so used1.
(2)	Individuals may subscribe to funds created for the purpose of meeting- the legitimate expenses of individual candidates, or the candidates in general, of any political party, subject to the following restrictions:
(a)	No such subscription may exceed- the sum of ten thousand dollars and must be of the personal money of the subscriber.
(b)	The candidate, or the person acting for such candidate, or the person acting for any political -party receiving such subscription, must acknowledge receipt of the same in writing, and within two weeks -of the same being received by him must publish the full name and address of the subscriber, and the amount subscribed by him, and whether the subscription is generally for the funds of any political party or for any special candidatae in the following manner:
(1)	If the subscription is received by any one acting for any political party, in the Canada Gazette and in a daily newspaper published in the ^capital of the province where said subscriber resides.
(2)	If the subscription is received by any candidate, or by any person acting for him, in the Canada Gazette and in a newspaper published- in the constituency in which the said candidate is a candidate.

(3') Any person who violates any of the provisions of this section, or is an accessory to any violation thereof, is guilty of an indictable offence and punishable as in this Act provided.
I admit that this resolution may be somewhat crude and may require some burnishing up, but I believe that legislation should be passed along these lines so that there may be a removal of the feeling which is widespread throughout the country that vast secret funds are subscribed for the benefit of .political parties and in connection with which consideration is expected after the election.

I should like to add a few observations to those made by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster). I was pleased to listen to ihis remarks, and I am almost prepared to hazard the opinion that he got the idea as a result of a visit he made to the West last Fall where he saw in operation the very plan he now proposes. I listened the other night to the minister (Mr. Guthrie) when he made, the declaration that he wished to see politics purified.
I believe he 'was absolutely sincere in making that statement and I am going to give him credit for sincerity. I want to state in this House that the principal reason why this plan was put into operation is that the people in the West came to believe, as the hon. member for Brome suggested, that large corporations and financial institutions had in the past-and I think no one will deny that-subscribed large amounts of money for the purpose of campaign funds which were used in practically every electoral district in Canada. The people said: We shall have no more of this; we shall pay the expenses of a candidate ourselves; rubber stamps have been sent in from other districts without the people's consent when fifteen or twenty men can go into a corner and nominate a candidate, and then weeks before the convention is called we are told that Tom Smith or John Jones is the candidate. The people are sick and tired of that sort of thing, and when such men are elected and come to Parliament, the people say: What right have we to call such and such an individual our candidate; we have none whatever. They also say: If we subscribe our small amounts-not the $10,000 to which the hon. gentleman referred, but their fifty cents and their dollar bills or their ten dollar bills then we shall have a legal right to call the candidate ours. That is purity of politics.
Oh, oh.

That is initiative on the part of the people and that is the big thing . that is coming into the political life of this country. The plan works out well in practice, and there is no desire for graft on the part of these people who can give their one dollar or two dollars or five dollars for the purpose of calling a candidate theirs, a right that was denied them in the past. I approve the sentiment expressed by the hon. member for Brome in his amendment.

I agree with the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) that it is the desire of every 'hon. member on either side of the House to endeavour to make elections as clean as possible, and I think that is our duty. But I cannot see, for the life of me, how it is legal for one man to subscribe and not another. If the president of a large concern wishes to give one thousand dollars or five thousand dollars, he can collect that from the other members of the concern and hand the money out as his own. If there is one thing that is worse than another as regards collections for election campaign funds, it is this-in several parts of the Dominion we have men going to every farm where they can get a dollar, from six months to a year and probably even two years before an election is expected to take place. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) says that we do not know who is to be the candidate, but a candidate will be selected. Is it fair or reasonable to go to the electors of this Dominion and ask them to subscribe money to assist a candidate to be elected when they do not know who is going to be brought out as a candidate? In western Canada, I am told on good authority that men now go from farmer to farmer asking them to subscribe so much when they do not know who the candidate is going to be. If some one is nominated, he may be dead before the election takes place. That is very unfair.	,
They are not obliged to give.

No. but they are told that this money is for election purposes. Why should a man give a contribution when he does not know who the candidate is going to be and when the latter may be some one to whom the man may be opposed?
I believe in clean elections; but my opinion is 'that every man should pay his own election expenses, and that a proper salary should be paid to every man in the Dominion of Canada whether he be a member of

Parliament, a civil servant, or even a judge, so that he may be able to pay his way, without having men going to the electors and asking for fifty cents here and ,a dollar there. I have been told that elections have taken place in Western Canada for which the printing alone has cost $4,000.
Will the hon. member mention one of those districts? *
I am told that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) said that it cost him $4,000 for printing alone'.
I will ask for the hon. member's authority.

most all my life, including five elections for this House. I was not always successful, but I can tell my friends of the United Farmers of Ontario that we did not spend thousands of dollars. We ran the elections economically, and we had clean, honest, upright elections. I think there is no more vicious kind of corruption than to have a man going around the country collecting one, two, three, four or five dollars and trying to buy men's votes. Let us be men; let us be honest; let us deal with this question in a reasonable way; let us fix a limit to the amount a candidate can spend in any riding, and let us prevent other persons from contributing in any way whatsoever. If we do that we may hope to have clean and honest elections. Just imagine two or three of the prominent people of a municipality going around soliciting funds for whatever amounts they can get, one, two, three, four or five dollars, and I do not suppose even five hundred dollars would be refused. I fully sympathize with the farmer. I have been fighting his battles for twenty-eight years and with some success. I was fighting his battles long before the United Farmers of Ontario ever thought of fighting them, but I must say, as a farmer myself, I am ashamed of some of the methods that have been adopted by some of the farmers' organizations. I wish to repeat that a limit should be placed on the amount that can be spent by a candidate in any riding, and I would make that limit very low and debar any contributions whatsoever from any individual, corporation, or society.

I am not aware that any very strong arguments have been advanced against the principle of small subscriptions and the interest they create throughout the country. The virtuous attitude that has been taken by some hon. gentlemen that they have not had this, that, or the other seems to me rather Puritanical. My hon. friend (Mr. Best) says that he has been credibly informed, that he has good authority for his statements, and so on, but he could not have better authority than myself as it was I who had all the experience out there in the West, and I am prepared to tell him what it was. His statement about spending $4,000 for printing is ridiculous, just as ridiculous as his statement that my campaign expenses were $12,000. I have here an audited statement giving my expenses in detail.
Read it.

It is rather lengthy. It
shows that the sum of $6,677 was collected, and quite a large proportion of that is still in our treasury. We spent over $2,000 in disassociating our political party from the Grain Growers' Association last summer. You can see that the campaign expenses therefore amounted to something less than $4,000; in fact it was nearer $3,000.
How much for incidentals?

It is all itemized here. The point I wish to make is this: the people of this country want publicity with regard to campaign funds-something they have never had before. We recognize that, and published a statement in detail.

How does the hon. member justify his' statement that nobody except himself knows what his election expenses were? Does he mean to say that I and other people have been making false statements about his expenses? I think his statement is unfair, and that the Puritan is on the other side. I published my expenses and I think my hon. friends here did too.

I understood the hon. member to say that $12,000 had been expended in an electoral district in the West. Now I am the only one member who has been elected on this platform in the West, and if the hon. gentleman was referring to the compaign expenses of any candidate in the West he must have been referring to me, and I repudiate his statement about my election expenses.

I did not make the statement that the hon. member's expenses were $12,000. What I said was that I had been informed-the hon. member made the statement himself within the walls of this House -that his expenses for printing were $4,000.
I said I supposed that would be more than one-third of the total expenses, which would make his total expenses $12,000 at least.
I did not say that $12,000 had been spent.

It is a nice distinction. I . want to repudiate the statement that I said it cost me $4,000 for printing. I did not make any such statement in this House, and you cannot find any record of it. I challenge my hon. friend to produce the proof.

Is this true? An extract
was handed to me to-day from the Regina Leader of January 2, 1920, showing the expenses of my hon. friend's election in As-siniboia divided under the heads of Organi-

nation and Campaign. It shows that $5,973.40 was disbursed. Is that correct? While I am on my feet, I may as well give the details. My hon. friend in conducting his campaign did not believe in giving particulars of his expenses, as is provided for in the schedule which he supported this afternoon. For instance, he gives under the head of Printing the amount of $457.10. " Sundries "-a very indefinite term in an election-$743.55; "Gould," whoever that is, $50; " Smith," another fine name in an election, $167; " General," another very gen-eial expression covering a multitude of sins, $361; "Gould," $360; "Smith," whoever he is, $331. Now, if my hon. friend will consider his attitude towards his own party-if it is a party-and the other parties, he cannot help but admit that he believes he belongs now' to an organization which is far and aw'ay superior to the others, the wicked political parties which have hitherto existed in this country-a party which is better morally and mentally and which, in a word, represents a clean-up of our politics. With an honest and candid man like my hon. friend, it is perfectly natural that when he gets on his feet he says what he thinks, and that is what he says to-day, the effect of his remarks being: We are going to show the country a new system of political finance, we are going to get fifty-cent subscriptions from all the people, and we are not going to accept large sums from corporations.
I am surprised to see that position taken to-day, because I remember, when, a week ago, this Bill was first in Committee, a nervousness manifested itself in the occupants of the seats opposite to me in regard to this clause. Apparently at that time my hon. friends felt that here was a weapon forged by their political enemies to destroy their activities. The clause was allowed to stand at that time, but I am convinced that my hon. friends then had the idea that they would oppose the clause, and I am fortified in that conviction by a statement made in the adjoining province of Alberta,-which I suppose has the same kind of organizations as are now trying to increase the following of my hon. friends; I presume my hon. friends will admit that this is their purpose. The statement I refer to is by Mr. P. P. Woodbridge, one time 'Secretary of the United Farmers of Alberta and still a member of that organization and of the United Grain Growers, and is contained in an interview in the Calgary Herald, as follows:
He does not by any means hold the same views as Mr. H. W. Woods-
Mr. Woods, I understand, is the President of the Alberta Association.
-regarding clause 10 of the new Dominion Franchise Act, which has of late attracted so much attention.
" Few who stop to think for a moment, or who are not too blindly prejudiced to wish to see for themselves," he remarked in the course of an interview with the Calgary Herald, " can fail to arrive at the conclusion that the clause in question is eminently fair and a step in the right direction towards true democracy and
control of the people's own affairs by the people themselves."
So, evidently, Mr. Woods, representing the United Farmers of Alberta, had begun to protest there, as a piece of propaganda, against the passing of this section. But I was glad to see that the hon. member for Bed Deer (Mr. Clark), who is associated with my hon. friend (Mr. Gould), when speaking in Toronto on Saturday last took a different ground, and apparently he has won over the others to his way of thinking. I think he was wise in coming to that conclusion, and I think they are wise in following his advice, because they would be doing a very dangerous thing to protest against a provision which they themselves had incorporated in their own platform.
Well, Mr. Woodbridge has some other interesting things to say. He continues:
The tendency of the United Farmers of Alberta under the spell of certain of its leaders has been to centralize all power of control over all- phases of the farmers' movement in this province into the hands of two or three men.
I leave it to my hon. friends to name the gentleman to whom Mr. Woodbridge refers -and I wonder whether the same sort of thing occurs in other provinces. I quote further:
The enforcement of this clause in the Franchise Act means that these men would be forced to separate themselves from the control and direction of the association proper or from that of its political branch. All their careful preparation and inspired eloquence which was so recently used to bring these two organizations under one control would be wasted.
The fact is, that under the influence of these leaders the organized farmers have in recent years adopted into their own organization one by one most of those practices which have encouraged the growth of the very evils and abuses which they so condemn amongst others. In this case their leaders are hoisted by their own petard, and that which will help to prevent the autocratic control of elections among their so-called enemies will also force a wider distribution of the responsibility in their own organization. It will serve to force a greater degree of local autonomy among the people themselves, and it will compel a more democratic alignment and division of the absolutely autocratic power at present exercised . by those leaders.
Well, I would not have dared to use such language as that, but when it comes from a gentleman who is ex-secretary and still a member, of the United Farmers of Alberta, I think it is proper that it should be made known not only to the province of Alberta but throughout the length and breadth of the Dominion. The point I am making-and I hope my hon. friends will take it good-naturedly-is that if the system.

under which they are now working, whether a system of individual subscriptions of fifty cents as pleaded for by the hon. member (Mr. Gould) or any other of the kind, is a financial scheme by which they as belonging almost exclusively to one class of labour or of occupation in the country raise campaign funds, then Ahat is a device which is a danger to the other classes of the community. I think that the country generally will agree with me when I say that. In theory it may be proper to have a definite system of finances by which enormous sums can be raised for elections, but in practice we *all know that it does not so work out. If, for instance, more than $6,000 was raised in Assiniboia by these fifty-cent subscriptions, that would mean that over 13,000 people contributed to this campaign fund-almost more adults than there are in the whole constituency. Of course, it is hardly likely that my hon. friend's opponents contributed to his scheme; so that he would have to make out a case based on the assumption that 13,000 people contributed to his campaign fund.
' Mr. GOULD: That is easy.

My hon. friend says that is easy. Well, we may have some mathematical calculations from him later, and if we do I hope he will explain how in a constituency of that size such an amount could be raised in that way, even if the people were inclined to subscribe. There are sixteen constituencies in Saskatchewan, and if the amount so subscribed was over $6,000 in Assiniboia, that would mean close on to $100,000 for the whole of Saskatchewan, and $1,500,000 for one particular party as respfects the whole Dominion. Will any hon. member be deluded into the idea that that large amount is to go into legitimate expenses? I do not care what may happen in Assiniboia; it may be all right; but if a million and a half dollars shall have been raised by any class party in this Dominion, there is a menace to the rest of the people of the country. While I do' not make any charges of corruption-I would be sorry to do so-I do say that it is for the rest of the country to take some notice of these patent facts and to protest against elections being run in this extraordinarily expensive manner. Now, Mr. Chairman, you will see how wide of the mark hon. gentlemen were who have been talking of $12,000 for the election and $4,000 for printing expenses alone. Surely when these figures are available to them on Hansard, when confronted with the real authority, they will act the Good Samaritan and state the facts as they really are rather than make statements with the object of making people believe things which they do not know to be absolutely correct.

Will my hon. friend
now answer the question I asked him a few moments ago about the recall?

The question is a very
fair one. We have that, as recorded in our platform. We believe in the principle of direct legislation. We also believe that with the initiative and the referendum you may have the recall. That is one of the planks of our platform, it is one of the things we discussed in our local. An agreement does exist between my committee, whose names I have read, and myself. Forty per cent of the number of- electors who voted at my election may, if I refuse to do what this committee asks me to do on the floor of this House-and that committee must meet very often and find out what public opinion is in the district of Assiniboia-if they advise me and I refuse 76|
to do that they can apply the recall, and ask me to go back. In going back I have the right of appearing before the people and giving an explanation of my attitude. The recall does not necessarily mean that they take the initiative away from me; in fact, it is both implied and actually writ-teen in my agreement with the committee that they do not wish to take the initiative away from me. I have given that agreement to my committee.
How many are on that committee?

It is an idea that has gradually attached itself to the principle of the recall. It is not correct to say that you place your resignation in the hands of a committee. I have not been asked to do that. Some of the members of my committee did put it that way, but after an explanation they could all see the reason why such a thing could not exist.

I do not see what object it would serve. We take the stand that any individual can make whatever agreement he likes. Nothing can prevent you having your private agreement with a committee or a man. I am very pleased to say that some planks of our platform have been adopted by this Government, and the day will come when the recall will also be adopted. Public opinion wilL oblige whatever government is in power to adopt that principle. That is my firm and honest belief, and I would not make a statement here that I believed to ba wrong. One of the arguments in favour

of it, one of the things that prompted people to suggest it, is that they have a distinct recollection of what they considered [DOT]was the political debauchery of this country during the reciprocity campaign. People believed that large sums of money were put up so that the powers that be could use them for the purpose of defeating the ends of reciprocity, and that this money was used for that purpose. The people want to do away with that, and I am pleased to stand here and record it as my opinion that if the Government are sincere in desiring to frame a measure that will clean up politics, they have in the publicity of campaign funds one of the greatest opportunities ever afforded a government to make themselves popular and also to clean up politics. If they want to clean up politics let them adopt the proposal which I now advocate in approval of the resolution put forward by the hon. member for Brome, make it 810 instead of $10,000.

The people's heart is right, and public opinion is going to carry this thing. You cannot stand in the way of public opinion. History records the fact that when public opinion takes a notion to do a thing you may legislate and legislate as much as you like but eventually public opinion will have its way, and those who have not kept pace with it must go down.
