I think it is absolutely necessary, especially after what we have heard this afternoon and this evening.

Just a word or two
more in connection with the clause before the committee. I am quite convinced tonight that the position I have taken with respect to this clause is absolutely right. I would therefore ask the mijnister if he would consider my recommendation and debar anybody from making a contribution for election purposes. In support of legislation of that kind we have had from the hon. member for Assiniboia to-night the best evidence that the committee could possibly wish for. The hon. gentleman has read a so-called statement, made he says by his financial agent. And what does it consist of? He claims to have handed out in various sums ranging up to $175 enough to buy an election in almost any riding in this country. The hon. gentleman did not tell us whether the persons who received this money were voters or non-voters. He has read a list of persons to whom payments were made-iMr. Jones, Mr. Brown, Mr. Wright, and so on. These persons received sums ranging from $10 up to $175. Are the persons to whom money has been so profusely handed outvoters? The hon. gentleman did not say that the expenditures were for printing, for working in the election, for running an aeroplane, for driving an automobile, or for any other purpose. He simply read a list of names sufficient to buy up-
I rise to a point of order.
Mr. 'Chairman, I have the floor.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for-Assiniboia has risen to state a point of order. He has the right to do so and I must ask the hon. member for East Peter-

borough (Mr. Sexsmith) to resume his seat until the point of order has been stated.
The hon. gentleman says I did not state where these moneys were expended. I maintained that I did.

That is not a
point of order.
The CHAIRMAN':	I must point out to
the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) that he has not stated a point of order. Any statement made by an hon. member can only be denied or corrected when he has concluded his remarks, unless he voluntarily relinquishes his right to the floor to enable another hon. member to make such denial or correction.

Mr. Chairman, I will leave it to the committee to say whether the hon. gentleman has in one single case, with respect to payments running from |20 up to $175 if you like, stated what the payment was for. That is the point. The Election Act demands that the financial agent of a candidate should publish a detailed statement of all the candidate's expenses showing what was done with the money, which statement must he itemized and certified to. I do not wish to offer any further remarks except to say this-and I want to emphasize it with all my power: The hon. member for Assiniboia, by his financial statement and by his speech, has produced the greatest possible evidence in favour of the enactment of an election law that will prohibit anything of the kind, for, according to his own statement, he may have brought those people to vote his way, and there is nothing in the statement affording proof to the contrary. He says, in effect, that Mr. Brown got $25, Mr. Jones $55 and Mr. Wright 1175; but he does not say what for. Now is that not corruption of the rankest and vilest kind? The hon. gentleman does not even mention the name of his typewriter or state what she was doing. I again appeal to the minister, and to hon. gentlemen on both sides, to join with me-to accept my proposition. Let us have an Election Act that will prevent the sort of corruption that we have heard so much about to-night from the hon. member for Assiniboia.

I wish to say a few words in regard to this section, and I can assure the committee that I am exceedingly surprised to find that it should meet with opposition from any group in this Chamber, especially the class of representatives who are supposed to speak for the agrarian in-[The Chairman.]
terest in the Dominion. Reading the section carefully I do not believe it contains a single word to which any person can take exception. It certainly refers to unincorporated associations and includes partnerships. It also refers to incorporated associations and incorporated corporations; but is there any justification for any unincorporated association, of any form, taking the assets of that business and distributing them amongst the various political parties in this country? It is very true that when you have a small partnership they may get together and may decide as a body that a portion of their funds shall be devoted for this purpose, and an unincorporated association may do the same; but when you have a large body of men I believe they will be restrained by any court of law if they undertake to dissipate their assets for the benefit of any political party. When you come to the question of incorporated corporations or associations there can be no doubt what the state of the law is. No corporation, no association which is incorporated, has the slightest power whatever to take and distribute its profits or its funds for the support or maintenance of any political party or on carrying on any political campaign. Do these hon. gentlemen wish to have the law in such a state that such men can go out and deliberately violate the obligations of their associates, their partners and their shareholders. I think the section should be enacted into law if only for the protection of those who are partners, associates, or shareholders in any of these firms or corporations in Canada. I have no doubt that the hon. gentlemen who are opposed to the section have seen in their advent into the political life of Canada the dawn of purity in politics but, as has been pointed out by hon. gentlemen sitting by my side, the figures which have been given by the hon. member for Assiniboia are astounding to every member of this House, and will he equally astounding to every elector throughout the length and breadth of the country. Ever since Confederation those who have been engaged in political life in the Dominion have been charged with insincerity upon the subject of campaign funds by men of the class to whom I have referred when they wished to impute impure or corrupt methods. But there has been no more foundation for charging the statesmen of the past with corruption than there is to charge the Agrarian party with intended corruption when they say they intend to raise a campaign fund of a million and a half of dol-

lars. The criticisms which have been made with regard to the financial statement given by the hon. member (Mr. Gould) are in my opinion absolutely just and very truly deserved. There is very little in that statement outside of the item for printing which would suggest how one single dollar of that money was spent.
We do not claim to be any purer than the farmers' party-and I have no doubt that the Liberal members of this House do not claim to be any purer,-but, Mr. Chairman, there is no reason why any faction should come into this House and charge the two great parties which have so successfully administered the affairs of the Dominion since 1867 with political corruption and defilement while they held their respective terms of office. If we wish to place our political life on a higher and nobler plane ,it will not be accomplished by pursuing the tactics which have been started in connection with this subject. So far as the Farmers' party, or the Labour party, or the Liberal party, or any other party which ,may be formed, is concerned, they have just as good a right to exist and to participate in the administration of our national affairs as any political party which has existed since Confederation. But, Mr. Chairman, their ideals must be higher, they must not be based on destructive political criticism, they cannot succeed if they hurl at other parties charges for which they have no more proof than they have/ submitted to this House to-night.
, I regret very much that I have not the pianuscript of the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), which is practically a substitute for this clause. It seems to me from hearing it read that it is worthy of very careful consideration by every hon. member. So far as the general principle of denying to associations, firms and corporations, unincorporated or incorporated, the right to contribute to political funds is concerned, I stand foursquare against such contributions, and I submit it is the duty of this Government to place some such legislation on our statute books.
There is another matter I would like to refer to-if you will permit me Mr. Chairman, for I think it is not exactly in order, but the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) has touched upon it and I think I may be pardoned if I refer to it briefly; it is the question of what practically amounts to the recall. He has referred to the electorate practically debauching members of the House of Commons in connection with campaign funds and the buying pf elections; but he stands up here to-night and admits that he has practically entered .into an agreement iwith his (electors in Assiniboia to resign in certain events. I know nothing which is more calculated to debauch our political life than such an agreement. It is true that this question has been discussed throughout the length and breadth of the West as to class legislation, "and it became an active issue in the province of Alberta during the last election. Frequent references have been made to the platform of the United Farmers of Alberta, and I do not purpose to go into that. But be that as it may, if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Gould) will deny that he stands for class representation, he must nevertheless answer or explain away that agreement to which he referred.
When one reflects that a member elected to this House is elected not for the constituency of Assiniboia, not for the city of Toronto, not for the city of Halifax, but as a representative of every man and woman in the whole Dominion, it is startling to find that in the face of that he immediately repudiates his obligations as a member of this House and says: I will not represent the Dominion of Canada, I will represent only the constituency of Assiniboia-and 'a very small-portion of the electors of that constituency.
If the hon. gentleman can point to any principle in the political history of this country which has a greater tendency to debauch and to stultify the representatives of the people, I certainly would like to have him tell us about it. And I do not limit my remarks to the hon. member for Assiniboia, but I include any other hon. members who will say that they are going to place a written resignation in the hands of a committee, to be acted upon iif they do not fulfil the wishes of that committee. What would be the effect? Members of Parliament, he tells us, are human. If any committee of his constituents can point a pistol at their representative's head and say: "If you do not vote thus and so we are going to place your resignation in the hands of the Speaker," what is that representative going to do? We are no more independent than those who are behind us make us, and when he feels that there is a possibility of losing his seat, just then he is going to obey the dictates of that committee, whether it be in the far East or in the far West. Supposing we approach a crisis in the affairs of the Dominion and perhaps twelve or fifteen votes in this House would turn the scale.

If those twelve or [fifteen men had this loaded pistol pointed at their heads, the destinies of this country might be changed for good or ill. I submit that that is a power which should rest in the people as a whole and not in any individual constituency or in any particular committee in that constituency. We must realize that when we sit in this House we do not sit here for the manufacturers, we do not sit here for the grain growers of the West, we do not' sit here for any class or faction, hut we sit here as representatives of all the people to pass legislation which shall contribute to the best interests of the country as a whole.
I am sorry that I have digressed, Mt. Chairman, but when the hon. gentleman brought this matter up I felt that I would be remiss in my duty if I did not refer to it. If there is no legislation on our statute books to meet this case, it is the duty of this Govefnment at this session to legislate that any agreement such as that referred to, entered into between a member and a committee of his constituents, is unlawful and shall have no bearing or influence on his conduct in this House.

It is said, Mr. Chairman,
that one cannot have an omelette without breaking eggs, and if in what I have now to say I should break one malodorous egg,* it will not be by accident, but by design. First of all, I believe in publicity of campaign subscriptions, but I see in it a measure of danger, which danger has not been pointed out in the discussion to-night. :So far as what has been said by some hon. members on this side of the House recently is concerned, I think their remarks about campaign subscriptions being a danger prove too much, for they prove that the man . who gives his services voluntarily in an election is a bad citizen. We all agree that that is nonsense. So too is the statement that money subscribed voluntarily for the support of a political cause is a public peril, and I cannot believe that men who assert it believe it.
. Now, with regard to campaign funds- and I have had about* thirty years' experience of elections and am not yet a very old man-I would like to know how many hon. members in this House can say on their word of honour that they believe their published campaign expenses cover all the moneys that were expended at their election. Now, there is what you are concealing, by the fact that you are-

I rise to a point of order. The hon. member is insinuating
[Mr. Tweedie. [
that the members of this House or some of them are dishonourable in the statements made of their campaign expenses.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If that was the intention of the hon. member I am sure that he will withdraw the insinuation.
Mr. DAV/IS: That was not my intention. Mr. Chairman. I said that these gentlemen would not give their word of honour that the sums shown by their statements were the only sums expended in their election. I do not mean that they knew what was otherwise expended or that they were parties to that expenditure. Nevertheless, there is scarcely a man in this House who does not suspect that sums were expended which came from a campaign fund, and that is what is struck at in the amendment submitted by the member for Brome. There is no use in camouflaging the situation ; we may as well face it honestly.	*
Nevertheless, this is what I say is objectionable and against public policy in connection with the publication of campaign subscriptions: A man of large means has just as much right to subscribe to a campaign fund as the man of small means. When you publish the fact that the man cl large means has subscribed to a campaign fund you at once excite comment on the part of opponents as to what this contributor expects for his large subscription. That man may have no more reasonable anticipation of favour because of his subscription than the man who has subscribed his two dollars, but if he has gone the limit mentioned by my hon. friend (Mr. Mc-Master), $ 10,000, it is undoubtedly a ground for comment. Perhaps some method should be devised by which the malodourous suspicion which now attaches to campaign funds may be allayed without arousing class feelings or embittering party politics. But for the present, if I have to choose between that danger and the benefits which in my opinion will result from publicity of campaign subscriptions, I shall vote for their publicity.
Mr. EDWARDS1: Mr. Chairman, I shall occupy only a few minutes of the time of the committee, as most of the things that I had in mind to say have been said better and more vigorously by the member for Calgary (Mr. Tweedie) than 1 could say them. I can understand why the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) has introduced this amendment. I had almost expected that the amendment would have been seconded by the member for South Renfrew

(Mr. Pedlow). The member for Brome had an opportunity of seeing the iniquities carried on jn the constituency of Assiniboia. He was there; he did not have to view them from a distance. He was right in the midst of this whirlpool of iniquity to which reference has been made by several hon. members, and practical admission of which has come from the hon. member who is in receipt of the honour produced by that iniquity. I can understand how keenly alive the hon. member for Brome is to the necessity for stringent regulations in our Franchise Act to put a stop to such terrible things as he must have witnessed in that campaign out in Assiniboia.
I hold in my hand a little document entitled "The New National Policy." I assume that some of my hon. friends on the other side have seen it; 1 do not know that it adds anything to the halo which surrounds the document that they take a pride in it. However, we will let that pass. In this document I find this paragraph:
And whereas the protective tarftX has heen and is the chief corrupting influence in our national life, because the protective interests, in order to maintain their unjust privileges, have contributed lavishly to political and campaign funds, thus encouraging both political parties to look to them for support, thereby lowering the standard of public morality.
This pronouncement is all the more significant in the light of what took place in the election in Assiniboia. According to this expression of opinion, politics in this country have been vastly corrupted by contributions to campaign funds. Yet we find a regular, systematized campaign carried on under the auspices of this holier-than-thou party to collect campaign funds, not from this and that individual, but systematically from door to door. /If they meant what they said when they placed that plank in their platform, they should have been the last persons in the world to seek to collect campaign funds for political purposes. There is this to be said in regard to contributions that have been made in former elections in this country; 1 have no doubt that contributions have been made by individuals, perhaps by corporations, manufacturing establishments, and so on, to both political parties, but I am not aware that contributions have ever been made by individuals, corporations, manufacturing establishments or any other group of men that carried with them a demand that the party or person for whom the contribution was made should step down and out whenever the contributor said so. If we accept
as true the statement that contributions have been made by corporations and manufacturing establishments in times past- and this clause in the Bill is aimed to put a stop to that-we know that these contributions have been made to this or that party because the contributor believed in the principles of that party; but it has remained for this holier-than-thou party to collect contributions from certain people in this country for the benefit of and to carry out the ' wishes of a certain class in this country. Never in the history of Canada, except through this organization, have contributions been made to either political party to carry out the wishes of a particular class and involving a penalty if those wishes should not be complied with. What else but class legislation can you expect from a party which is tied up as this party is? The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) told us to-night that there was in his constituency a special committee composed of fifteen men; that this special committee met regularly to pass their opinions upon his acts and his conduct in this House; that he might expect to hear from this special committee of fifteen if his conduct and his votes in tins House did not meet with their approval; and that when this special committee of fifteen intimated to him that his course was not acceptable to them, they had the right to ask him to step down and out;-or at least, when forty per cent of the votes cast in that constituency made that demand, he had to comply with that demand, and step down and out. I should like to ask the hon. member for Assiniboia if he will place on the records of this House the agreement which he signed with the fifteen men on that committee. The hon. gentleman sits in this House as an elected representative of what? I want to know; I have a right to know; the people of this country want to know. Does he sit here as the elected representative of the people of the Dominion of Canada or as the elected representative of a group of people situated in Assiniboia?
' Disqualify him on his own statement.
I do not know but that the remark of my hon. friend (Mr. Butts) is quite in order. I should like to see the agreement before saying whether hjs statement is in order or not.
You are only a doctor.

I admit this is a matter - for the diagnosis of a lawyer rather than that of a doctor; but coming back to the

remark of the hon.' member for Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Butts) we have an hon. member holding a seat in this House who says that he has signed an agreement which is held by fifteen men out in Assiniboia;-and I claim that having referred to that agreement, having acknowledged that there is an agreement signed by him and held by that committee, that hon. gentleman is in duty bound to place [DOT]that agreement upon the pages of Hansard. If that does not come pretty close to an in-. fringement of the Independence of Parliament Act, then I want to know what do,'s. 'What would he the result in this country if this condition of affairs obtained throughout the whole of the Dominion of Canada.
We would have an election.

That might not be just as favourable to the hon. member (Mr. Maharg) as he thinks. It might even have the result of sending my hon. friend back to rely upon his $5,000 or $6,000 that he does not get in this House, and that he does not get out of farming except by farming the farmers. Let me just say this to my hon. friend who seems quite certain of himself and of his little group, that I will venture the proposition that when the next election takes place, that group will be even smaller than it is now, because just as soon as the people of this country have an opportunity of seeing behind the doors and investigating the platform and policy of these hon. gentlemen, the people will have enough sense to turn them down and to make their choice between the two old parties which have carried this country on since Confederation.
What about Timiska-ming?

I do not know that my ' hon. friends in the little special group on the other side are cheering or feeling very gay over that. I have not seen any very strong manifestations of pleasure on their part over the result in Timiskaming. Of course, I suppose that they are willing to claim this man, now that he has been elected, but they were mighty careful to keep away from him while the election was on. Probably, if they had gone up there, they would have had to come to some conclusion and state definitely where they stood as regard the eight-hour day proposition. They hedged in regard to that when the matter came up in this House, and they said that it was "forced for strategic pur poses"-I think that was the term which

one hon. gentleman used in regard to it. They did not express themselves upon the eight-hour day proposition; for .strategic purposes, it was better to remain silent so that they could maintain the cohesion between labour and the farmers. Had they gone to Timiskaming, they might have required to answer those questions, and so they kept away. In regard to that election, however, they can take all the comfort they like out of it and I do not think any hon. member on either side of this House wall begrudge them the candidate who was elected in Timiskaming.
Does the hon. member know the figures of that election,-whether the candidate who was elected beat the other two?
He did not. In fact, 1 believe the vote polled was about half of that which was polled in the previous election.
Six of one and half a dozen of the other.

Somewhere about that. It seems to me, in regard to this case, that what we are asked to consider is this. Do we intend, by the adoption of this clause, to put a stop to any contributions, by corporations or unincorporated companies or organizations, to parties for political purposes? That is the question before us. We have the statement in the platform of the United Farmers or Grain Growers that they believe that in times past there has been corruption from that sodrce, yet we find them opposing this clause which is designed to put a stop, so far as it is possible for Parliament to do so, to corrupt practises.
Is it not a fact that this clause was in the old Act? There is no change in it.

It seems to me that the only way in which we can get on the track of our hon. friends opposite is to take it for granted that they are as holy and pure as they say they are and to make an exception of the United Grain Growers or Farmers in this clause.
You are taking big chances.

I have no doubt that in that case the clause would go through without further opposition. That is no doubt what these hon. gentlemen would like; but I want to say that from the standpoint of electoral purity, there never before was an instance in the whole history of the

Dominion of Canada which made so much for corruption and debauching of the electorate as these systematic methods, adopted by this new group over the way, and we have only in imagination to apply their methods to every constituency in the Dominion of Canada, to realize just how corrupting and debauching the methods which they advocate would be to this country. It is the bounden duty of this Parliament to enact restrictions that will prevent these gentlemen from carrying out the methods which they have declared as their own.

It was not my intenion
to intervene in this debate, and I would not have done so but for the endeavour that has been made on the opposite side of the Ho use, apparently deliberat ely as Hansard will	show to-morrow if it is carefully followed, to prove that we have been opposing clause 10. The hon. member (Mr. Edwards) made the statement that the Grain Growers' representatives were opposing clause 10. That was an absolute mistake. Nobody in this group has said that he was opposed to section 10 or to its principle. On the contrary, we heartily endorse this principle, every word of it. The only suggestion that was made from this quarter was for the insertion of two words "organization or" referring to incorporation, and I think the hon. member who offered the suggestion made his position perfectly clear.
Does the hon. member speak for the official Opposition?

No, I am speaking for those whom the hon. member (Mr. Edwards) saw fit to describe as the grain growers' representatives. There may be some of those people in the official Opposition. At all events, there are no doubt members of the Opposition who would like to be representatives of the grain growers because they know what the results would be.
I wish to deal briefly with the arguments of my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards) who has just taken his seat. He said that he could quite understand the reason why the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) moved his amendment, because he had had practical experience of the evils he was trying to remedy. My hon. friend must know that the amendment is absolutely copied from the system that was adopted in Assiniboia. It was individual contributions that were made in Assiniboia, and that is what this amendment calls for, if I understand it, and individual contributions only. So his argument there falls absolutely to the
ground. It is interesting and very significant to note the great desire for political uplift, if I might use the term, that has been in evidence since the agriculturists and the ordinary people of Canada decided to take some interest in the affairs of the country, even to the extent of spending a little bit of their money in an effort lo improve conditions.
We have heard references to. a "Disgusted Grain Grower," and I could not help wondering if it were not possible that some of the statements that have been made here had their foundation in disgusted politicians. Personally,. I pay very little attention to anonymous contributions to the press. If a man has not the backbone to put his signature to the views he wishes to put before the public, I think the public is justified in paying very little attention to them. My hon. friend (Mr. Mowat) made a most significant statement this evening. He said that the expense of an election in a city was about ten times greater than that of an election in a rural district. I cannot for the life of me understand how he reaches that conclusion. Some of our rural constituencies are from one hundred to one-hundred-and-fifty miles square, and are fully settled. Does he mean to say that you can cover that territory at less expense than you can cover a city constituency where you can walk from one end to the other in perhaps fifteen minutes? Or does he mean to suggest that it takes a lot more money to bring the people in a city constituency into line with the proper view than the people in the country? I do not know on which of these alternatives he bases his ten-to-one calculation, but certainly it cannot be that the renting of halls for meetings in a city, where thousands of people attend, or transportation expenses in a constituency which you can cover on foot in less than an hour, accounts for this difference. There must be some other feature peculiar to a city election if it costs ten times as much to conduct as an election in the country.
My hon. friend laid great stress on an article that he said was written by Mr. Woodbridge. If he had not told this House the position that Mr. Woodbridge had formerly held, it might have passed, but he told us that Mr. Woodbridge was a former secretary of a farmers' organization, and we know it is quite customary for deposed individuals as well as deposed politicians to find fault.
My hon. friend (Mr. Gould) put on Hansard to-day a statement of his election ex-

penses. One or two members have claimed that he made no reference at all to the pry-poses for which these moneys were to be expended, but simply gave names of individuals. Surely that must be a deliberate mis-statement, for my hon. friend (Mr. Gould) stated distinctly that these items were for the expenses of . speakers during the campaign. He made that very clear, and surely the hon. gentlemen who undertook to castigate him in that respect were very wide of the mark. Their objections were quite uncalled for. All we ask is fair play. We do not want anything else. We have absolutely nothing to hide. We court the fullest investigation into every dollar of expenditure and every dollar of contribution.
Coming now to clause 10, I have stated that we are not opposed in any way to the principle, but personally, if I have to choose between the clause as it now stands, with no provision made to cover the points raised by my hon. friend (Mr. McMaster), I shall have to vote for the amendment. The amendment deals with what is perhaps of more vital importance than anything contained in the Bill. It demands the immediate- publication of all contributions towards campaign funds. That I regard as of vital importance, and unless the minister in charge of the Bill is prepared to give us an undertaking that this clause will be amended to provide for the full publication of all contributions to campaign funds I shall be compelled to vote for the amendment. I think the minister would be well advised to give us such an undertaking.
We have heard considerable from the other side of the House about the recall. I shall not go into that very fully to-night. The principle of the recall has been recognized for years* and years. As my hon. friend (Mr..Gould) has stated, if over forty per cent of the voters who actually voted at his election are dissatisfied with his actions they can recall him. I am not prepared to say that there is anything vicious about that principle. I am of opinion that if that principle were in force to-day we would probably not require resolutions in this House calling for an election; I am fully convinced that we would have had one long ago if that principle had been in effect. I agree with hon. members in the opinion that we ought to have campaign funds if the people are to be represented by those whom they desire to represent them. But if you compel each candidate to defray all his election expenses, then I think you will succeed in establishing here a rich man's

club and will not make for the proper representation of the people. I think the principle is sound that the people should pay their own way. It. is their business and their business only, and it is only fair that when their business is being conducted they themselves should pay all the expenses in connection with it. We stand by that principle as a sound one, as one which tends to the general improvement of political conditions in the country, and we are absolutely opposed to contributions being made from industrial concerns, whatever they may be. But we do not think there can be any serious objection to the principle that the voters themselves should contribute the necessary expenses to carry on an election campaign.

The hon. member (Mr. Maharg) strongly emphasizes the importance of the virtues of honesty and fairness on the part of members of this House and of the people generally throughout the country. Permit me to say, Mr. Chairman, that I do not concede to the farmers or the manufacturers, or any other class of citizens in Canada, a monopoly of the fairness and honesty that characterize the nation. These virtues should be remembered by all the associates of the hon. gentleman in making such statements, for instance, as that said to have been made by a gentleman, at Timiskaming who, I understand, alleged that it cost forty per cent of the Victory Loans to float the loans. The hon. member at the beginning of his remarks made the statement that none of his party had taken exception to this clause 10. Well, the press is very badly misquoting the* hon. member and some of his friends, for I will read an item from a newspaper report which does not accord with the statement of the hon. member. This item is dated Toronto, March 24, and is as follows:
The proposed Federal Franchise Act occupied the attention of the delegates to the annual convention of the Canadian Council of Agriculture here to-day, and it was the expressed belief of the council that clause 10 of the new Act would interfere with the legitimate political activity of organized farmers.
Clause 10 provides that no company or association, unless incorporated for political purposes. may contribute to political funds.
It was the opinion of the council that any organization, incorporated or otherwise, should be permitted to contribute to political funds, but that in all cases the source of such contributions should he made known before an election takes place.
John F. Reid, M.P., Torkton, Saskatchewan, and John A. Maharg, M. P., Moosejaw, Sask., made statements to the effect that the clause as drawn would prevent contributions by farmers' organizations to campaign funds for political

purposes. The fear was expressed that the clause might even debar the Canadian Council of Agriculture from issuing campaign literature, as this would be for a " political " purpose.
I can hardly see wherein this extract coincides with the hon. gentleman's assertion that there was no objection on the part of any members of his party to this clause.
Camouflage.

I know that the hon.
gentleman wants to be fair, and perhaps he will accept my correction. In referring to the clause, I sajd that none of us had made any objection. That is to say, none of the members of this House had made any objection to the principle of the clause.

Of course, I accept the hon. gentleman's correction, but I think he is a little more guarded in his words now than he was on the former occasion. In regard to the question of recall, I do not think any hon. gentleman in this House, who gives the subject any thought, can consider the proposition a fair one. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) criticized the campaign funds of past elections, and I should like to ask him this question: Would he consider it fair for my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), for example, to be elected to this House, using part of the campaign funds of the party he represents and offering, let us suppose, to the Manufacturers' Association the privilege of recalling him if he did not support what they chose to propose in regard to the tariff? Yet that is just as fair as the proposition that some of the farmers of the country put up. The farmers, after all, do not constitute the whole population of the country. There are a few other classes besides the agricultural communities, and I made it my. business to ascertain just what was the proportion of each class of citizens in Canada at the census of 1911. The census showed by occupations in the category of those earning their living, farmers 993,735-34 per cent of the population; manufacturers, that is, people working in factories, 491,342; and-

Will the hon. gentleman be good enough to give us the exact information in regard to the farmers as he has given in regard to the manufacturers? There are a number of people who make their living by employment in agriculture, and the number quoted by my hon. friend represents those who are actually farmers.
Air. . MANION: The hon. gentleman evidently is under the impression that I am
endeavouring to mislead the committee. Let me inform him, however, that I am giving the exact proportions as shown by the census of 1911, and those engaged in the manufacturing industry are given as 491,342, or eighteen per cent of the population. But the interesting point, and the one that touches me personally-for I am neither a farmer nor a manufacturer, but a member of the middle class-is the fact that the great mass of the working population do not belong to either of the foregoing classes and totals 1,298,557, or forty-eight per cent. In other words, the farmers make up thirty-four per cent, the manufacturers eighteen per cent, and the others, including myself, men of other professions, labourers, etc., forty-eight per cent, practically half of the total. I must say therefore that it is about time that this forty-eight per cent got busy, and I intend to take my part in an effort to see that the manufacturers and the farmers shall not entirely run the affairs of the country. That is the point I wish to make. I do not think that the farmers of this country, even if they are a fairly strong party, should feel that they are the whole poulation of Canada, as some seem to think; they should remember that sixty-six per cent of the workers of the country are not farmers.

I should not have risen had it not been for the honour which has fallen to this group in the House of holding the attention of the opposite side for such a length of time, I think it is a great credit to us in this small group that we have had so much attention accorded us, and I cannot help feeling that hon. members in the other opposition will feel grateful to us for having contrived to give them a much-needed rest. Some days ago I rose in my place to reply to the hon. member for East Peterborough (Mr. Sexsmith), and was not allowed to go on at the time, 'being assured that the question would come up again when I should have an opportunity of discussing it. However, I do not think I shall ''spend any time to-night replying to the hon. member; I shall leave the matter to the decision of the electors, and when the time comes the hon. member will get his answer.
Now, I desire to answer a question that has been asked by an hon. member on the other side as to what would happen if we had the recall in effect. I tell him that if the recall were in effect there would not he enough left of hon. members opposite to form a corporal's guard.
Oh, oh.
No wonder they are scared of it.

Some hon. gentlemen
have objected, and objected very strongly, to our raising a campaign fund by voluntary contributions. Those of us on the cross benches seem to be a thorn in the flesh of hon. gentlemen opposite. Our presence in this Chamber must occasion them great pain judging from the agonizing groans which they emit from time to time.
In criticizing our method of collecting money to meet election expenses the hon. member for East Peterborough (Mr. Sex-smith) declared it was disgraceful and very humiliating to see the farmers' organization collecting funds voluntarily and publicly, and he spoke of going around with a basket for these funds. Well, all I can say is, the farmers in East Peterborough must have contributed very lavishly when it required a basket to hold the collection. Hon. gentlemen opposite, if they are sincere, must also object to the method of raising funds for the Forward Movement in connection with the churches. As I say that was a Forward Movement, and ours is a Forward Movement also.
I am very sorry to think that the few members in our little parliamentary group have caused hon. gentlemen opposite so much annoyance. At the same time we cannot help it. We were elected just as they were by the votes of the people in the ridings that we represent, and consequently we have as much right to our seats in this Chamber as have the hon. members who have been indulging in the criticisms referred to. We are only a small group as yet, and there are always some bullies who will abuse the small boy, but the time comes when the small boy reaches manhood. This "small boy,'' if I may speak of our party as such, will eventually grow up and take the places of hon. gentlemen opposite. Our representatives have commenced to arrive and they are still coming.
It was suggested during the discussion that these men who gave subscriptions were buying votes. I must say that I never before heard of a man buying his own vote with his own money.
I will not occupy any further time of the committee, except to say in closing that all hon. gentlemen opposite need to do is to keep on abusing the farmers, because we are thriving on that abuse. My advice to them is to keep on putting up all the obstacles they possibly can in our path; they are only, driving the nails deeper into their own political coffins.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the amendment carry?
Before the amendment carries-
Oh, oh.

-and in so stating I merely compliment the intelligence of the members of the committee-1 would crave the indulgence of hon. gentlemen for a moment in order to present the gist of the amendment I have moved, because when I submitted the amendment in the first place a large number of hon. gentlemen who are now sitting in the Chamber were not present. First of all, the amendment is not in any way opposed to the principle of the clause as it appears in the Bill; it merely goes further than the clause does. The clause states that no unincorporated company or association, and no incorporated company or association other than one incorporated for political purposes alone, shall make contributions for political purposes. My view is that under this clause nothing would be easier for any body, association or company, who wished to contribute heavily to campaign funds, than to organize a small corporation for political purposes only, and then for that corporation so organized to subscribe to the campaign fund of any of the parties or of individual candidates. My amendment goes still further. I leave out the specific clause about companies or corporations incorporated for political purposes alone, and my amendment reads that no incorporated or unincorporated company or association, nor any firm, shall directly or indirectly contribute to campaign funds. I will not bother reading the exact terms of the resolution; they are almost word for word with the terms of the clause as it appears in the Bill. Then I go on to say that individuals may subscribe to funds, either to the general fund of any of the political parties or for any individual candidate, but I say that these individual subscriptions must be subjected to certain restrictions, and I have made the restriction that there shall be no contribution larger than $10,000.
Shame!

I am free to say that amount may be too large and I am willing to make it smaller. But I know that there are here and there in the country rich men who, with pure motives, do subscribe very heavily to campaign funds. The

second restriction is that there shall be full publicity to- all campaign subscriptions, whether to the party generally or to individual candidates. That is the gist of my amendment.
Now that amendment was not inspired through my visit to Assiniboia. I have a very distinct recollection of that visit, and even were the recollection likely to fade hon. gentlemen opposite constantly remind me of the trip. Well, it was a most enjoyable trip. It is true, I was not successful, but I learned a great deal about the West. I had the pleasure of addressing audiences than whom none could have been more intelligent, patient, or courteous, and I came back with a very high appreciation of the people of the West. I did my best to elect the Liberal candidate in that riding.
I am sorry I was not successful. But I would not allow this occasion to pass without raising by voice in protest against the charge made by hon. gentlemen opposite that the candidate won by corrupt methods, because in my humble opinion he did not do anything of the sort. What did I find when I went out to Assiniboia? I found that the people of Assiniboia were so anxious to elect the Grain Grower candidate that they were not only prepared to work voluntarily, but to put up their own money, to return him. Now is that a wrong thing to do?
No.

You cannot imagine
that in a constituency like Assiniboia a man of modest means is going to be able to meet his own election expenses, because that riding is as big as some of our Eastern Provinces. It would take a man days, if not months, to go from place to place. And, of course, there are all sorts of other legitimate expenses. Unless we are prepared to say that only rich men can enter this House we have got to have some way of meeting such cases. In a large riding such as Assiniboia-I represent a riding Where a man of modest means can meet his own election expenses-or in populous cities like Toronto or Montreal, it is almost impossible for a candidate of modest means to meet his own expenses. Now what is the remedy? Which is best to have-money coming in from outside, from a central fund subscribed by we know not whom, to be spent in the riding; or is it best for the electors to put their hands in their pockets and subscribe to the legitimate expenses of the candidate in that riding. I prefer the latter method. It is true it is open to objection. I found
that a lot of the people of Assiniboia were pf Scotch descent-*
, Some hon. MEMBERS: Oh, oh.

-and Irish descent too, and the old verse was brought to my mind very strongly, that "Where your treasure ;,s there shall your heart be also." I found that after putting up $2 or $3 or $4 or $5- or 50 cents, as the case might be, to help their candidate, it was very difficult for pie to get them to vote: otherwise, although jbey might be perfectly convinced that my arguments were better-without saying a word about the candidates, because comparisons are odious.
, That is an objection it is true, for it makes the man who has subscribed for the election of a certain candidate a stronger partisan than he otherwise would be. But ps between the constituency in which the electors individually put up their money to elect their candidate, and the constituency in which men wait for their day's time to be paid from outside funds, I prefer the former, although I do see the disadvantages. As far as I could judge there was nothing but extreme partisanship aroused ,by individuals contributing ito the election of their candidate in the constituency of Assiniboia. I would ask hon. members to believe that there was no corruption; that these payments which have been read by ,the member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) were made to a certain number of speakers, for I saw them, I heard some of them, and although I do not know whether they were pll worth the money that was spent upon them, I do know that they were speaking for the candidate.
! Now, why cannot this amendment be accepted? I believe it is a slight improve-pent on the law, and I would ask the (House to support it.

speechtext: What I object to is making it legal for a man to subscribe $10,000 even to one candidate, for it sets the stamp of approval on any man putting up that amount to elect a candidate, and if 'he does so, he is bound to have a certain amount of influence over .that candidate when elected.

It never has been found .necessary in Canada to place any limitation on the subscriptions of an individual; but it has been found necessary in our political history and in the wisdom of this House to place restrictions upon what corporations might be disposed to subscribe for political purposes. In the year 1908 .the House of Commons passed clause 10 almost in the identical language in which it .appears in the Bill to-day. So if my hon. friends from Assinibo-ia (Mr. Gould) and from Maple Creek ,(Mr. Maharg) imagine that the clause was passed with reference to the Grain Growers of Saskatchewan or the United Farmers of Ontario, they are very much astray in theiir conclusions. The clause was passed for the avowed purpose of putting .a stop ito corporate- subscriptions for election purposes, and I believe it has done good .service since it was enacted. The

proposal of the Government is simply to re-enact -the -clause in this Bill. In fact, the only change of language is -that which occur-s in the first line to make it quite clear that its real application is to corporations and associations, be they incorporated or unincorporated.
I understand there is a consensus of opinion in this House as to the propriety of this clause remaining. Then why not let us all vote for it? "Oh no," my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) says, without reading the statute or the Bill-
I have read the statute and the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
-and he comes forward with an amendment to provide for something that is absolutely provided for in the Bill, and provided for, I think, by a method much better than his proposal. Why, this afternoon, those who paid any attention to what was going on in this House know that we passed a most drastic clause, to provide for publication of every subscription that is given for any political purposes durilig an election. We provided in .the'most ample way for the publication of these facts. If hon. members will turn to clause 79 of the Bill-and this was all read this afternoon-they will find that the following information must be furnished:
Within two months after the election all moneys, securities, and the equivalent of money, received, by or promised to the official agent or the candidate or any other person for the purpose of expenses incurred, or to he incurred, on account of or in respect of the conduct or management of the election, naming every person from whom the same may have been received, or by whom such promise was made, showing as to each sum whether it was received or merely promised, whether in money or otherwise, and whether as contribution, loan, advance, deposit or otherwise.
All that information has to be given, and it must be published in a newspaper in the constituency -where the election took place. That is a much more comprehensive section than the amendment submitted in the resolution of my hon. friend from iBrome. Any man who wanted to circumvent the law could circumvent that amendment, for there are other ways of paying money than by a direct cash payment. This clause is the result of experience in this country and in Great Britain, and it is designed to meet not . only every direct payment or contribution, but every indirect payment or contribution, and every promise to be hereafter kept, whether by way of contribution, loan, advance, deposit or otherwise. It will afford far more efficient relief than is provided for in the proposal of my hon.

friend. The only thing in his proposal that raises a new subject for discussion is the $10,000 limitation. We have never had a limitation in Canada upon individual subscriptions. If the committee think it well to provide one, I do not think there is any serious objection to doing so. But I do not know that we have ever been very much bothered in our political contests by $10,000 subscriptions from individuals. I have never heard of any.

What about the Pacific
scandal, when $100,000 was paid into a campaign fund?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Some exception has
been taken by hon. members on this side to that part of the clause which provides, in effect, that contributions may be made for political purposes by companies or associations incorporated for political purposes only. That clause was much discussed in the session of 1908. The language was first introduced at that time, and the Conservative party of that day contested it most strongly. Sir Allen Aylesworth who, as Attorney General in the administration of that day, had charge of the Bill, boldly said, speaking on the subject in the House, that that clause had been introduced to protect the Liberal Association of Ontario, which was an incorporated political association; and he said that he had no doubt that there were Conservative associations in Canada which were likewise incorporated. He maintained the right of these associations, which were organized purely for political purposes, to contribute to the political cause which they supported. Now, I understand that in British Columbia there are one or two political associations that have been incorporated. Certainly the Ontario Liberal Association is an incorporated association under the law of Ontario. It is not a trading corporation; it is not an association which is out for gain or reward; it is purely an association for political purposes, for educational purposes, if you like, and as such its right to take part in elections was maintained by Sir Allan Aylesworth in these particular words which appear in elause 10. I may tell you that the Government does not care one whit whether or not these words are struck out from the third line of the clause. The clause has been taken just as it appeared in the old
law, and in my opinion the old law worked well. We have maintained the old law; we have provided for more stringently than has been suggested by any one else against improper subscriptions. We have made provision for publicity; we have tried to meet the evil intent of all persons who would try to hid or cover up their subscriptions. I do not know that any body could ask us to go very much farther. The object has been to provide an absolute safeguard. But this section deals only with corporate subscriptions. I ask the committee to pass it, and if they want the publicity clauses further improved when we come to them, let us improve them. I do not think that we should mix two subjects in one section.

What is the section
which deals with the publication of contributions?

When I spoke before, I was desirous of bringing certain matters to the attention of the minister, and I gathered that my first suggestion at least has not been favourably received by him. I have been endeavouring for some time to catch your eye, Mr. Chairman, but the minister who has charge of this Bill got in ahead of me at my last effort. It was not my intention to say anything on this subject to-night, but I must not overlook the pressing invitation given to me a little earlier in the evening by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards). He seems to speak with a certain amount of cocksureness on every occasion and upon every subject, but let me inform him that in this case he has another guess coming. Several speakers have made reference to a certain political contest that took place last fall in Saskatchewan, and I think it is only proper that I should reply in a mea. sure and somewhat endorse the very flattering remarks made by my confrere on that occasion, the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), who has to-night given expression to his opinion in regard to the reception accorded to him and myself at that time. speechtext: I must remind the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) that if we wander into any other constituency than Assiniboia, I am sure we Shall not be able to register any progress to-night. .

I bow, of course, to the
ruling of the Chair; but it is only fair, as this matter has been referred to so often to-night and on so many other occasions than to-night, that I should be allowed the privilege of replying in some measure to the remarks that have been made.
As regards the clause that is under discussion at the moment, the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) has suggested' that it is only to be expected that I should second the amendment moved by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster). Let

me tell that hon. gentleman that the amendment has been seconded already by another hon. member on this side of the House, the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Fournier). If I were to express my private conviction upon this subject, I would move an amendment to the amendment along this line, and I think this amendment to the amendment would find an echo in the minds of not only a number of members on this side, hut of quite a few on the Government side. I might preface the reading of the proposition I have in mind by calling attention to a statement made by my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards). He asked the -question: Do we intend to put a stop to contributions to campaign funds from any source, to stop corrupt practices? In my judgment, there is only one way to stop a thing, and that is to shut it off altogether, not to try to make an easy or partial remedy, but to treat it in a straightforward manner. The terms of my suggested amendment to the amendment would read in this manner: That contributions for political purposes, by any person, organization, incorporated or unincorporated company or association fee absolutely prohibited, and that any person, organization, incorporated or unincorporated company or association violating this provision is guilty of an indictable offence against this Act, punishable as in this Act provided.
Is the hon. member prepared to cut out corrupt practices?

If the hon. member had listened patiently to my amendment, the question he asks would have been answered; speaking personally, I have no need to answer his question; I am speaking for general application only. The amendment I have suggested represents my feelings in this matter; but I gather from the tenor of the addresses given here to-night, that the preference is for the amendment moved by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. MoMaster), and I shall have much pleasure in supporting that amendment.

May I be permitted to offer a thought, not with the expectation of any immediate result, but merely for the purpose of dropping a seed which, one of these days, will come to maturity? There is a solution of this question, although I believe neither the Government, nor the House, nor public opinion is prepared to adopt it at present; but I believe that in this progressive age-and I wish it to be understood that in the best sense of the word I am a Progressive-the time is not far distant when all the necessary legiti-77*
mate expenses of an election will be, as they should be, a proper charge on the treasury of the Dominion. The election of a member of Parliament is not necessarily for his personal advantage; it is not necessarily for any local advantage; it is necessary for the peace, order and good government of this Dominion, and the time is not far distant when, under proper conditions,, the treasury of Canada will bear, as it should, all legitimate expenses.- Of course, it will then be necessary to prescribe the character of the expenses and to limit the amount. But I want to offer the thought, not with the expectation of any immediate result, but in the belief that some who, like myself, are still amongst the youngsters, will live to see the day when we shall get rid of all such questions as this by making these legitimate expenses a proper charge on the Dominion treasury. Then there will be no question whether a candidate shall spend a sum large or small j every sum spent outside of the official expenditure, by an unauthorized agent, will be illegal. If this does not come about in the near future, still I think that some day it will be done.
